claims.text: The predictive model explicitly incorporates defect states, including 1 wt.% oxygen contamination.
The model represents the effects of defects and oxygen on electron scattering in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Quantum and defect scattering dominate the electrical conductivity behavior of HfNbTaTiZr in the nearly 0–200 K regime.
Phonon scattering is the primary conductivity-limiting process in HfNbTaTiZr from 300 to 1200 K.
The defect-aware model will predict conductivity more accurately than analytical methods that assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
The studied material includes bulk HfNbTaTiZr and a controlled variant containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Oxygen produces modifications to the electronic structure that are relevant to conductivity prediction.
Conductivity experiments are conducted on both nearly pure and 1 wt.% oxygen-contaminated HfNbTaTiZr samples.
Defect structures and oxygen-related local electronic perturbations increase electron scattering relative to a perfect crystal.
Explicitly modeling defect and oxygen effects on electronic density of states and scattering rates reduces systematic conductivity-prediction errors.
At low temperature, enhanced defect scattering accounts for additional electrical resistivity.
At high temperature, conductivity depends on an interplay between oxygen-induced carrier scattering and phonon interactions.
In the 0–200 K range, conductivity will be lower than defect-free estimates.
In the 300–1200 K range, incorporating oxygen effects will alter the predicted temperature dependence and reduce prediction error.
Conventional analytical conductivity models ignore oxygen contamination and assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Conventional analytical models often overestimate conductivity when significant defect scattering is present.
The model is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with homogeneous defects and oxygen contents up to 1 wt.%.
The model is expected to remain valid from near 0 K to 1200 K.
The model may require modification for nanostructured samples or oxygen contents substantially different from 1 wt.%.
Oxygen contamination can occur within the bulk or subsurface phases of refractory Nb-based alloys.
